section.title: Prayer for the Ephesians
section.sectionRationale: Resuming the sentence he broke off in 3:1, Paul kneels before the Father and prays for the church he has just described as one new humanity and a dwelling place for God. His petition matches his theology: that the God whose fullness fills the temple would strengthen these believers by the Spirit, so that Christ dwells in their hearts and they grasp the immeasurable love of Christ and are filled with all the fullness of God. The section closes chapters one to three with a soaring doxology to the God who does far more than we can ask or imagine.
section.thesis: Paul bows before the Father and asks that out of His glorious riches He would strengthen the Ephesians by the Spirit in their inner being, so that Christ dwells in their hearts by faith and they, rooted in love, come with all the saints to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge and are filled with all the fullness of God, closing in praise to the God who can do immeasurably more than we ask or imagine.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Paul kneels before the Father from whom every family is named; the petition for inner strength, Christ's indwelling, and being rooted in love; the prayer to know the surpassing love of Christ and be filled with God's fullness; and the closing doxology to the God who does immeasurably more.

units.label: Paul kneels before the Father
units.note: from whom every family is named

verses.text: ... for this reason I bow my knees before the Father,
from whom every {{patria|family}} in heaven and on earth derives its name.

units.label: Strengthened, indwelt, rooted in love
units.note: power by the Spirit, Christ in the heart

verses.text: I ask that out of the riches of His glory He may {{krataioo|strengthen}} you with power through His Spirit in your inner being,
so that Christ may {{katoikeo|dwell}} in your hearts through faith. Then you, being rooted and grounded in {{agape|love}},

units.label: The love that surpasses knowledge, filled with God

verses.text: will have power, together with all the saints, to comprehend the length and width and height and depth
of the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, that you may be {{pleroo|filled}} with all the fullness of God.

units.label: Doxology
units.note: to Him who does immeasurably more

verses.text: Now to Him who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, according to His power that is at work within us,
to Him be the {{doxa|glory}} in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

patria.gloss: A family, clan, or line of descent, a group deriving its name and identity from a common father. The word plays on the Father, pater, in verse 14: every patria in heaven and on earth takes its very name from Him. God is not merely one father among many but the source of all fatherhood and family, the one from whom every household, angelic and human, derives its being and its name.

krataioo.gloss: To strengthen, to make strong or mighty, to empower. Paul asks that God would krataioo the believers with power in the inner being, the hidden self, by His Spirit. This is not strength for outward feats but inward might: the deep fortifying of the soul so that Christ may make His home there and the vast love of Christ may be grasped and borne.

katoikeo.gloss: To dwell, to settle down and take up permanent residence, as opposed to a passing stay. Paul prays that Christ may katoikeo in their hearts through faith, not visit as a guest but live at home there, at the very centre of the person. It echoes the temple imagery of 2:22: the God who dwells among His people also dwells within each heart where Christ is welcomed by faith.

agape.gloss: Love, specifically the self-giving, sacrificial love that God is and that God pours out, supremely shown in Christ. Paul prays that believers, rooted and grounded in this love like a tree planted deep and a building set on firm foundation, would come to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge. It is at once the soil we grow from and the immeasurable reality we are called to comprehend.

pleroo.gloss: To fill, to make full, to bring to completeness. The prayer climbs to its height here: that believers may be filled with all the fullness of God, saturated with His own life and love and character. It does not mean becoming God, but being flooded with the moral and relational fullness of God, the very fullness that dwells in Christ, 1:23 and Colossians 2:9, now filling His people.

doxa.gloss: Glory, weight, splendour, the radiant worth and honour that belong to God. The doxology ascribes doxa to God in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations. The same glorious riches from which He strengthens His people, verse 16, return to Him as praise, and remarkably the church, the reconciled temple, becomes a place where His glory is displayed and celebrated forever.

basic.context: Paul now finishes the prayer he began in verse 1. He kneels before the Father, the source of every family in heaven and on earth, and asks four great things: that God would strengthen these believers by His Spirit in their inmost being, that Christ would settle down and live in their hearts by faith, that, rooted in love, they would grasp with all the saints the vast love of Christ that is beyond knowing, and that they would be filled with all the fullness of God. He ends with a burst of praise to the God who can do far more than we ask or imagine.
basic.hermeneutics: The prayer resumes the broken sentence of verse 1, marked by the opening ellipsis. It is a single flowing petition built on the word so that: God strengthens us so that Christ dwells in us, so that we comprehend His love, so that we are filled with God's fullness. Each request leads to the next and climbs to the fullness of God, then overflows into the doxology of verses 20 and 21, the seam that closes the first half of the letter.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul kneels before the Father from whom every patria, family, is named, a play on the word Father. He asks God to krataioo, strengthen, them inwardly by the Spirit, so that Christ may katoikeo, take up permanent residence, in their hearts. Rooted in agape, love, they are to know the love of Christ and be pleroo, filled, with all the fullness of God. The doxology renders all doxa, glory, to Him in the church and in Christ Jesus forever.
basic.typology: The temple where God dwelt is fulfilled twice over here: Christ dwells within the believer's heart, and the church is filled with the fullness of God, the true sanctuary of His presence. The glory that once filled the tabernacle and temple now fills a people, and returns to God as praise from the church throughout all generations.
basic.christ: Christ stands at the centre of the prayer: He dwells in the heart by faith, His love is the immeasurable reality believers are to know, and the doxology ascribes glory to God in Christ Jesus forever. The fullness of God that fills His people is the same fullness that dwells in Christ. To be strengthened inwardly is, at heart, to have Christ make His home within.
basic.god: God is the Father from whom all fatherhood and family derive their name, rich in glory, generous in strength, and able to do immeasurably more than we ask or imagine. He is the God who fills His people with His own fullness and works His power within them. The whole prayer rests on His abundance: it is out of the riches of His glory that He gives, and to Him all glory returns.
basic.crossReferences: Colossians 2 says the whole fullness of deity dwells in Christ, and you have been filled in Him. Ephesians 1 speaks of the church as the fullness of Him who fills all in all. John 14 promises that the Father and the Son will make their home with those who love Christ. Romans 8 speaks of the Spirit strengthening believers within.
basic.oneStory: The story that ran from a garden where God walked with man, through a tabernacle and temple filled with His glory, reaches a new depth here: God now dwells within His people by the Spirit and Christ makes His home in the heart. The presence once fenced behind a veil now fills a reconciled people who are being filled with all the fullness of God, and the whole movement overflows into glory given to Him forever.

context.literary:
This prayer is the second of two in the first half of Ephesians, and the two are meant to be read together. The first, 1:15 to 23, asks that the eyes of the heart be enlightened to know hope, inheritance and power. The second asks for strength, indwelling, love and fullness. Each ends in a surge toward Christ's lordship or God's glory, and each is a single sentence in the Greek that twists and climbs.

The structure is a staircase of purpose clauses. After the address in verse 14 and the grounding in verse 15, Paul states his petition in verse 16, 'that out of the riches of His glory He may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being'. A string of 'so that' clauses follows, and each one is the goal of the one before it. The strengthening is for the dwelling of Christ, the dwelling is for the grasping of love, and the grasping is for the fullness of God. Verse 18 has a pair of participles, 'rooted and grounded', that stand outside the main flow like a supporting beam, one an image from agriculture and the other from building. They describe the condition in which the requests are answered.

Then the prayer breaks into doxology in verses 20 and 21. It grows from 'ask' to 'ask or imagine', and from 'all' to 'so much more than all'. The 'throughout all generations, forever and ever' echoes the 'age to come' of 1:21 and marks the close of chapters 1 to 3. The doxology works as a seam: chapters 1 to 3 say what God has done, and from 4:1 Paul will say how to live in it. The word 'therefore' there depends on this prayer.
context.historical:
Paul's posture is itself information. Kneeling in prayer is not the most common posture in the Jewish world, where people stood to pray, as in 1 Kings 8:22 and Luke 18:11, though kneeling is known for intense or urgent prayer, as at 1 Kings 8:54 and Luke 22:41. Paul's words 'I bow my knees' suggest an earnest and humble approach, and the context is a prison cell.

The prayer is also set against the background of a city that believed in many powers. Ephesus was known for its worship of Artemis and for magical practices, and Acts 19:19 records the burning of expensive magic books after Paul's ministry there. Converts from this world might have feared hostile spiritual forces and wondered about the reach of the God they had come to trust. Paul prays that they will know the full extent of Christ's love and be strengthened with power through the Spirit, which answers the fear in the most basic terms.

'Every family in heaven and on earth' is also meaningful for readers who lived in a world where family, clan and city decided one's name and status. In the ancient world a father's name carried a family's identity and its honour. Paul says every family, whether human or heavenly, takes its identity from the Father, and so the Gentile believers who had no family line to the people of God are named by the same Father.
context.canonical:
Paul's prayer draws from the great Old Testament blessings and praises. The blessing of Numbers 6:24 to 26 asks that the LORD bless and keep His people, make His face shine on them and give them peace. Paul asks for more than blessing; he asks for the indwelling of Christ. Behind 'rooted and grounded in love' lies the Old Testament contrast between the tree planted by water, Jeremiah 17:8, and the dwelling built on rock.

The measuring of dimensions recalls Job 11:7 to 9, where Zophar asks whether we can fathom the deep things of God, and the reply is that they are higher than the heavens and deeper than Sheol. Paul's answer to that question is that there is a way of knowing what cannot be measured, through love. Psalm 103:11 compares God's loving devotion to the height of heaven above earth, and Psalm 36:5 to 9 sets it among the highest mountains and the deepest sea.

In the New Testament the prayer sits alongside Romans 8:15 to 16, where the Spirit assures believers that God is their Father, and John 14:23, where Jesus says that He and the Father will come and make a home with anyone who loves Him. It also parallels Colossians 1:9 to 12 and Philippians 1:9 to 11, two other Pauline prayers. The doxology belongs with Romans 11:33 to 36 and Jude 24 to 25, which ends a letter with the same blend of power and praise.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is not telling the Ephesians what to do; he is telling them what he asks God to do. That is the first thing to see. He knows that his teaching of chapters 1 to 3 is not enough by itself, and that understanding God's plan is not the same as being strong in it. So he turns from instruction to intercession, and the readers are meant to overhear and learn how to pray for one another.

The prayer is also meant to correct a common misreading. Having been told in chapter 2 that salvation is by grace and that they are fully included, the Ephesians might suppose that nothing more remains. Paul says there is more: strength, an indwelling Christ, a grasp of love that goes beyond understanding, and fullness. The prayer sets before them what Christian growth looks like, and it frames it as something God gives, not something believers must produce.

Finally, Paul intends the doxology to give his readers a sense of scale. He has asked for great things, and then he says God can do far more than that. He wants them to pray boldly, without limiting their requests to what seems likely, and to look back at what God has already done as the measure of what He can still do.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a prayer, so it is neither a command nor a plain narrative; it is a model. Paul reports what he asks for these particular believers, and we may not assume that every believer will have the same experience in the same order. But the request is also a pattern for what we may rightly ask for ourselves and others, since the same Spirit and the same Christ are at work in all God's people.

Two cautions follow. First, the dimensions of verse 18 are not given as a technique. Paul does not say the readers should meditate to measure the love of Christ; he says God must give the power to comprehend it. Second, 'filled with all the fullness of God' should not be read as saying that believers become God or that they reach a final state in this life. The verbs are petitions, and the passage looks toward a completion that Paul sees as still to come, as the church grows toward 'the full measure of the stature of Christ' in 4:13.

The doxology, by contrast, is a statement of fact: God is able to do far more. That belongs to every believer's confidence, and it is why the prayer is something to imitate, as Christians pray not only for relief but for strength, love and the knowledge of Christ.

debates.question: What are the 'length and width and height and depth' of verse 18?

views.label: The dimensions of Christ's love
views.case: The verse says believers will comprehend these dimensions 'to know this love that surpasses knowledge', so the object is the love of Christ. The four dimensions give an image of immensity: it is long enough to last through all time, wide enough to reach all peoples, high enough to reach the heavens and deep enough to reach the lowest. This is the most natural reading, and it suits Psalm 103:11, which measures God's devotion by the height of the heavens.

views.label: The dimensions of God's wisdom, mystery or plan
views.case: Some commentators connect the measurement with the wisdom and mystery of the preceding verses, 3:10, and note that Job 11:7 to 9 speaks of God's depths in similar terms. On this view the dimensions refer to the whole scope of God's saving plan in Christ, of which the love of Christ is the heart.

views.label: The shape of the cross
views.case: A very old tradition, found among some church fathers, sees the four directions as the arms and posts of the cross. It is an attractive picture, but the text gives no sign of it, and most interpreters regard it as a devotional reflection and not as Paul's meaning.

debates.bearing: The first two readings are close, since God's plan is the outworking of Christ's love. What matters is that the thing measured cannot actually be measured, and that Paul prays for a knowing that goes beyond knowledge.

debates.question: What does 'every family in heaven and on earth' refer to?

views.label: All of God's creatures, angelic and human, grouped in families
views.case: The Greek patria means a family or clan descended from one father, and Paul says every such group in heaven and on earth is named from the Father. This takes in angelic orders as well as human families and nations, and is consistent with 1:21, which speaks of every rule and authority and every name that is named.

views.label: The one family of God, believers living and departed
views.case: Others take Paul to mean the church, with believers on earth and those who have died and are in heaven forming a single household of God. This fits the language of 2:19, 'members of God's household', and Hebrews 12:22 to 23.

debates.bearing: Either reading makes the same pastoral point: no family, human or heavenly, has an independent origin, and the Gentile believers who thought they had no family now belong to the one the Father names.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's petition in verse 16 uses dynamis, 'power', and in the same verse speaks of the 'inner being', literally the inner man, esso anthropos. The phrase also appears in Romans 7:22 and, in a related form, in 2 Corinthians 4:16, where the outer man wastes away while the inner man is renewed day by day. The point is that strength is given where the believer is weakest, in the self that no one else sees.

The two images of verse 18 are rizoo and themelioo, 'rooted' and 'grounded', both in the perfect tense. The perfect describes a state that has been established and continues. The first word comes from the field and the second from the building site, so the believer is pictured as both a plant with deep roots and a house with a firm foundation. Notice that both are passive: believers do not root or ground themselves. Colossians 2:7 has a related pair when it speaks of being rooted and built up in Christ.

Katalabesthai, 'to comprehend', in verse 18 is a verb that can mean to seize or take hold of, and in some contexts to grasp with the mind. John 1:5 uses it of the darkness that has not overcome the light. Here it carries the sense of taking a firm hold, which suits the paradox that follows: the love of Christ is known, yet it hyperballei, 'surpasses', knowledge. This is a verb of overshooting, to throw beyond. Paul prays that people will know something that outruns knowing, which means that real knowledge here is not mastery but trusting acquaintance, as when we say we know a person without exhausting them.

The doxology piles up comparatives. Verse 20 says God is able to do 'hyper panta', above all things, and then adds hyper ekperissou, 'beyond all measure', literally something like more than superabundantly. The English 'so much more than all we ask or imagine' tries to capture the double stretch. Paul uses a similar construction in 1 Thessalonians 3:10 and 5:13.

Notice finally the tense of verse 20, where the power 'is at work' within us. The participle energoumenen is present and ongoing, and it comes from the same root as the English word energy. The power that raised Christ, 1:19 to 20, is not stored for later but active now in believers.

In verse 21 the doxology gives glory 'in the church and in Christ Jesus', two spheres joined by a single 'and'. The church and Christ are named together, and the phrase 'to all generations of the age of the ages' stacks plural words for time, an attempt to say that praise has no end.

typology.fulfillment: God's presence settled in the tabernacle, Exodus 40:34 to 35, and in the temple, 1 Kings 8:10 to 11, but Solomon himself asked whether God could dwell on earth when the highest heaven cannot contain Him, 1 Kings 8:27. Paul prays that Christ may dwell in the hearts of believers. The verb for dwell suggests settling in as a permanent resident. John 14:23 records Jesus' promise that He and the Father will make a home with those who love Him, and 2 Corinthians 6:16 calls believers the temple of the living God. The type falls short in that the old dwelling was a place; the new dwelling is a person within persons, and no longer needs a building.

typology.type: The Father who names families, Ephesians 3:14 to 15
typology.fulfillment: In the Old Testament God names His people and gives them a place in a family, as when He renames Abram and gives him a promise of many nations, Genesis 17:5. The pattern is a father who gives a name and a place. Paul says that every family in heaven and on earth is named from the Father. The escalation is from one family line to every family. The type falls short in that earthly fatherhood is partial, and Paul says all such naming comes from the original source, so earthly fathers are shadows and not the standard.

typology.type: The boundless dimensions of God's dwelling, Ephesians 3:18
typology.fulfillment: The ideal temple vision of Ezekiel 40 to 48 is full of measurements, a rod of precise length laid on every wall and gate. Revelation 21:15 to 16 shows an angel measuring the city and finding its length, width and height equal. Paul's prayer asks for the power to grasp dimensions that cannot be counted. The correspondence is between measured sacred space and a love that is more than measure. The type falls short because the measured temple was an architectural form, while what is measured here is the love of Christ, which is beyond any plan.

typology.type: Blessing that goes beyond the request, Ephesians 3:20
typology.fulfillment: Solomon asked God for wisdom and received riches and honour as well, 1 Kings 3:11 to 13, and Abraham's servant who prayed for a wife for Isaac received far more, Genesis 24:12 to 27. These small stories show a God who exceeds requests. The escalation in Christ is that God gives His own Son and Spirit, Romans 8:32. Paul's doxology says the same: He does more than all we ask or imagine. The type falls short because Solomon's gifts were earthly, while the gift Paul prays for is the fullness of God.

study.christ:
Christ is the subject of the prayer's central petition, 'that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith'. Everything before it prepares for that, and everything after it flows from it. It is easy to read this verse as a general wish for spiritual health, but Paul is specific: his prayer is that the risen and ascended Lord will take up residence in believers, which he says elsewhere is the mystery, 'Christ in you, the hope of glory', Colossians 1:27. The promise of John 14:23 is thereby carried into the church's life.

The prayer is addressed to the Father, but its second half concerns the love of Christ. This love is the content of the knowledge Paul prays for, and its dimensions are measured by what Christ has done. Galatians 2:20 says that He loved me and gave Himself for me, and Romans 5:8 says God proves His love in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners. The dimensions of verse 18 can be traced on the cross, where the love that reached the farthest and the lowest, to the death of a cursed man, is shown. This is the one place where the unmeasurable has been measured.

The fullness Paul asks for is the fullness of God, and Colossians 2:9 to 10 says that in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form, and that believers have been made complete in Him. The prayer is therefore not asking for something outside Christ. To be filled with the fullness of God is to be filled from the one in whom the fullness lives, and John 1:16 speaks of receiving grace upon grace from His fullness.

Christ also appears at the end, in the doxology: glory is to be given to God 'in the church and in Christ Jesus'. He is the mediator through whom the Father is praised, as Jude 25 says, and the one in whom the church's praise reaches the Father. It is Christ's presence in His people that makes their worship possible.

One caution: the indwelling of Christ is not a new addition to the Spirit's work. Verse 16 asks for strength through the Spirit, and verse 17 asks for Christ's dwelling, so the Spirit is the way Christ is present, as Romans 8:9 to 11 shows when it moves without a break between the Spirit of God, the Spirit of Christ and Christ in you.
study.god:
The prayer shows God in three persons at work in one believer. The Father is the one before whom Paul kneels and from whom all family takes its name, the Spirit is the means of strengthening, and Christ is the one who dwells. This is not a doctrine of the Trinity stated in the abstract, but the Trinity as the shape of Christian experience: God gives, God dwells and God fills.

God is shown first as rich. He acts 'out of the riches of His glory', not from them as a rich man might give a small coin out of his wealth. The preposition means that the supply is drawn from an inexhaustible store and the gift is proportioned to it. Philippians 4:19 puts the same truth plainly: my God will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus.

God is also the source of all families, which means that He is the origin of fatherhood itself. The Father is not a human father enlarged. Human fathers are patterned on Him. For anyone whose experience of fathers is painful, this is good news, since the standard of fatherhood is not the failing example but the Father who strengthens, welcomes and fills.

The doxology gives two attributes at once. God is able, meaning that He has the power to do immeasurably more, and He works in us, meaning that His power is near and not remote. The same God who raised Christ from the dead, 1:19 to 20, is the one at work within us, and Romans 8:11 makes the connection explicit. Power and nearness belong together.

The passage also shows how God relates to human knowing. God's love surpasses knowledge, and yet He wants His people to know it. This holds together two truths that might be thought to conflict: God is beyond our full grasp, and He is not hidden. Job 11:7 asks whether we can fathom God, and Paul's answer is that we cannot comprehend Him fully but can know Him truly, by love, and that He gives the strength to do so. That is also a guide to worship. We do not come to master God but to be filled with Him, and the right response to what exceeds understanding is praise, as Romans 11:33 to 36 shows.

Finally, God's glory is meant to be returned. The glory 'in the church' goes up to God through the lives and praise of His people through all generations. The Father who gives out of His glory receives glory back, and so the prayer ends where it began, with the Father.

crossReferences.note: The first of Paul's two prayers in the letter, asking that the eyes of the heart be enlightened to know hope, inheritance and power. It asks for knowing; the second prayer asks for strength and love. Read together they cover both the head and the heart, and each rests on God's power at work in believers.

Another Pauline prayer with several shared elements: knowledge of God's will, strengthening with all power according to His glorious might, and thanks to the Father. It shows that the requests of Ephesians 3 are representative of how Paul prays for churches generally.

The Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry 'Abba, Father', testifies with our spirit that we are God's children. This gives the ground of Ephesians 3:14: the one before whom Paul kneels is a Father to believers, and the Spirit makes that known within them.

Jesus says that if anyone loves Him, the Father will love him and 'We will come to him and make Our home with him'. It is the closest gospel parallel to Christ dwelling in the heart, and shows that Paul's prayer asks for what Jesus promised.

Zophar asks whether anyone can fathom the deep things of God, using the same four directions, higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth, wider than the sea. Paul reverses the despair of the question: the unmeasurable is something to be known by love.

The LORD's loving devotion reaches to the heavens, His righteousness is like the highest mountains and His judgments like the deepest sea. The psalm ends with feasting on His abundance and drinking from a river of delights, which suits Paul's prayer for believers to be filled.

In Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form, and believers have been made complete in Him. This explains where the 'fullness of God' of Ephesians 3:19 is found. It is not a separate supply, but the fullness that rests in Christ and is shared with His people.

God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. It is the experiential side of Ephesians 3:16 to 19: the Spirit makes the love of Christ known within, so that knowing it is not only an idea but a gift.

Solomon asks whether God will really dwell on earth when even the highest heaven cannot contain Him. Ephesians 3:17 answers by saying that Christ dwells in the hearts of believers, so the answer to Solomon's question is a people and not a building.

Paul bursts into praise at the depth of God's riches, wisdom and knowledge, whose judgments are unsearchable and whose ways are untraceable. It ends with 'to Him be the glory forever', a close parallel to the doxology of Ephesians 3:21.

A doxology to the one who is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them unblemished in His glorious presence. It shares the 'able' of Ephesians 3:20 and shows that God's ability is the standard biblical ground for praise at the end of a letter.

God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying 'Abba, Father'. It explains how the three persons act together in the prayer: the Father sends, the Spirit of the Son is in the heart, and the believer calls out to the Father in confidence.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with God filling a world and placing human beings in it to bear His image and share His life. In the garden He walks with them, Genesis 3:8. The fall breaks that fellowship, and the story of Scripture is the story of God finding a way to dwell again with His people. The tabernacle, Exodus 40:34 to 35, and then the temple, 1 Kings 8:10 to 11, are His first answers: glory fills a building. But both are only a foretaste, and Solomon himself says heaven cannot contain God, 1 Kings 8:27.

The prophets promised more. Ezekiel 36:26 to 27 promises a new heart and God's own Spirit within His people, and Ezekiel 37:27 says His dwelling place will be with them. Jeremiah 31:33 promises that the law will be written on their hearts. The fulfilment is the sending of the Son and the Spirit. At Pentecost the Spirit fills the believers, Acts 2:4, and from then on the dwelling place of God is not a building but a people.

Paul's prayer stands at this point in the story. It asks that what God has already done, making a people His dwelling, be known and experienced in depth. It describes a life of love rooted and grounded, with the love of Christ as the climate in which the believer lives. It also fits the larger plan of Ephesians 1:10, to bring all things together in Christ, since the one who is filled and fills is at work in the church for the sake of all things.

The story ends where the prayer points. Revelation 21:3 says that God's dwelling is with man, and Revelation 21:22 says that there is no temple in the city because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. The believer's partial knowing becomes full, 1 Corinthians 13:12. What Paul asks for in a prison cell is a glimpse of what the whole creation will be filled with, as Habakkuk 2:14 foretells, when the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say he bows his knees before the Father?

options.text: As an act of earnest reverence before the Father from whom every family is named.
options.note: Kneeling signals unusual earnestness; God is the source of all fatherhood and family.

options.text: Because kneeling was the only permitted posture for prayer.
options.note: The usual posture was standing; kneeling here marks special earnestness.

options.text: To draw attention to his own piety before others.
options.note: The focus is on the Father and the church's need, not on Paul's display.

options.text: Because the Father is only one family head among many equals.
options.note: Every family in heaven and on earth derives its name from Him; He is the source of all.

quiz.q: What is the first thing Paul asks God to do for the believers?

options.text: To strengthen them with power through His Spirit in their inner being.
options.note: The prayer begins with inward strengthening, out of the riches of His glory.

options.text: To give them outward success and comfort in daily life.
options.note: The request is for inner might by the Spirit, not outward ease.

options.text: To remove all suffering from their lives at once.
options.note: Paul prays for strength within; he has just called his own sufferings their glory.

options.text: To make them wealthy and powerful in the eyes of the world.
options.note: The power sought is inward, by the Spirit, so Christ may dwell within.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean when he prays that Christ may dwell in their hearts?

options.text: That Christ would take up permanent residence at the centre of their lives through faith.
options.note: The word means to settle and live at home, not to pay a passing visit.

options.text: That Christ would occasionally visit them as a guest.
options.note: The word means permanent residence, not an occasional visit.

options.text: That they would simply think about Christ from time to time.
options.note: Paul asks for a deep indwelling by faith, not mere occasional reflection.

options.text: That Christ dwells only in the church building.
options.note: Christ dwells in the hearts of believers, echoing the living temple of 2:22.

quiz.q: What does Paul pray they would come to know together with all the saints?

options.text: The love of Christ in its length, width, height, and depth, which surpasses knowledge.
options.note: The immeasurable love of Christ is to be grasped in community with all the saints.

options.text: The exact date of Christ's return.
options.note: The object of the prayer is the love of Christ, not hidden timetables.

options.text: A secret knowledge reserved for a spiritual elite.
options.note: It is grasped together with all the saints, not by an elite few.

options.text: That God's love can be fully mastered by human intellect.
options.note: This love surpasses knowledge even as we are called to know it.

quiz.q: What does being filled with all the fullness of God mean?

options.text: Being saturated with God's own life, love, and character, made like Him yet not becoming deity.
options.note: Believers are flooded with the fullness that dwells in Christ, transformed into His likeness.

options.text: Becoming divine and ceasing to be creatures.
options.note: The creature is filled with God, not fused into God; we remain His creatures.

options.text: Gaining unlimited earthly power and success.
options.note: The fullness is moral and relational, God's own character and presence.

options.text: Having nothing more to do with God's Spirit.
options.note: The filling is precisely the work of God's Spirit within His people.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe God in the closing doxology?

options.text: Able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, by His power at work within us.
options.note: The doxology exalts God's boundless ability and His power already working in believers.

options.text: Able to grant only what we can clearly picture in advance.
options.note: He does immeasurably more than we ask or imagine, beyond our picturing.

options.text: Distant and uninvolved in the life of the church.
options.note: His power is at work within us, and He is glorified in the church.

options.text: Deserving of glory for a single generation only.
options.note: Glory is given to Him throughout all generations, forever and ever.

questions: Paul prays first for inner strength, not outward ease. How would your own prayers change if you asked God most of all to strengthen your inner being by His Spirit?
Christ dwelling in the heart means settling in as a permanent resident, not a guest. What parts of your life have you kept as rooms Christ is not yet welcome to live in?
The love of Christ surpasses knowledge, yet Paul prays we would know it with all the saints. Why do you think grasping this love is something we do together rather than alone?
Paul asks that we be filled with all the fullness of God. What would it look like, this week, to live as someone being flooded with God's own life and love?
The doxology says God can do immeasurably more than we ask or imagine. Where have you been praying too small, and how does this truth enlarge your expectation of God?

translationNotes.note: The verse opens with an ellipsis in the BSB because Paul resumes here the sentence he began in 3:1 and interrupted with the digression of verses 2 to 13.
Family renders patria, which plays on pater, Father: every family or clan derives its name from the Father, who is the source of all fatherhood in heaven and on earth.

The love of Christ that surpasses knowledge yet is to be known holds together a real, growing grasp of that love with its inexhaustible greatness; the goal is to be filled with all the fullness of God, transformed into His likeness rather than turned into deity.

meta.notes: BSB text for Ephesians 3:14-21 reproduced as supplied, including the ellipsis at the start of verse 14.
